task_description:
Given a real GitHub issue and the project's codebase at the commit where the issue was
filed, an automated technique attempts to generate a test that reproduces the bug
described in the issue.
candidate_definition: ONE instance = ONE merged pull request that closes a reported issue and, in the same PR, adds or modifies at least one test that fails at the commit before the PR merged and passes at the commit that merged it. The instance is identified by {repository URL, merge_commit} where merge_commit is the commit that merged the PR (produced by any of GitHub's three merge styles: merge commit, squash, or rebase) and base_commit is merge_commit's FIRST parent. A single-parent merging commit (squash/rebase) is a normal, valid candidate; a second parent is never required.
data_source:
Real, public Python projects with an issue tracker and pull requests. ONE instance = ONE
merged pull request, identified by {repository URL, the commit that merged it}. Candidate =
a merged pull request that closes an issue and, in the same PR, adds or modifies a test: that
test fails when run against the commit before the PR was merged and passes when run against
the commit that merged it.

HOW THE PULL REQUEST WAS MERGED DOES NOT MATTER, and the instance must not require one style
over another. GitHub offers three merge buttons and projects differ: a merge commit has two
parents, the PR's work on the second; a squash merge and a rebase merge land the PR as ONE
ORDINARY COMMIT with a single parent. All three are valid candidates here. In every case the
merging commit is the postfix side and its FIRST PARENT is the base commit, which is the
prefix side -- for a squashed or rebased PR the first parent is simply its only parent. Do
not require the merging commit to have a second parent: that clause alone excludes every
project that squashes, which is a large share of the Python ecosystem. The two commits are recorded
under the names merge_commit (the commit that merged the pull request) and base_commit
(its first parent), whichever of the three merge styles produced them.

admissibility.name: commit_count
admissibility.observe: git rev-list --count HEAD in a full clone

constraints:
- Python projects only
- project must NOT be one of the 12 repos SWE-bench/SWT-Bench already use: astropy/astropy,
  django/django, matplotlib/matplotlib, mwaskom/seaborn, pallets/flask, psf/requests,
  pydata/xarray, pylint-dev/pylint, pytest-dev/pytest, scikit-learn/scikit-learn,
  sphinx-doc/sphinx, sympy/sympy
criteria:
- real merged pull request that closes a reported issue, merged in any of the three ways
  GitHub offers (merge commit, squash, rebase); the merging commit's first parent is the
  base commit in all three, and a single-parent merging commit is normal, not a defect
- the PR's own added/modified test fails on the pre-fix commit and passes on the PR's
  merge commit, confirmed by an actual test run
- both the pre-fix and post-fix snapshots build/install and run their test suite

- the builder verifies itself, by running it on its own machine, that the PR's test fails on
  the prefix version and passes on the postfix version, and that the PR changes non-test
  source; it records the test's id and its judgment in builder_notes
- done means: the harness ran every script on a blank machine without a crash, and the builder
  has verified the points above itself and written what it verified, with the numbers and the
  reason for anything it accepted against the harness's observations, into instance.json under
  builder_notes. The harness reports what it observed; the builder judges.
territory: Search for Python repositories with stars between 100 and 299 inclusive.
sibling_territories: Search for Python repositories with stars between 300 and 999 inclusive.
Search for Python repositories with stars between 1000 and 4999 inclusive.
Search for Python repositories with stars 5000 or more.
